newsitem.title: USA: Gun ruling puts spotlight on computerized system.
newsitem.headline: Gun ruling puts spotlight on computerized system.

text.p: The National Rifle Association on Sunday criticised the Justice Department for failing to swiftly push ahead in computerizing state criminal records for background checks on prospective gun buyers.
On Friday, the Supreme Court struck down a part of the Brady gun control law that required local sheriffs to conduct background checks on prospective gun buyers.

The NRA, the nation's most powerful gun lobby, seized on the ruling as evidence that the state criminal records of felons and fugitives should be computerized for gun checks, and the five-day waiting period discontinued.

"You have kids running around with computers and video games and the technology is more complicated than what it would take to get some of these police records at the state level off paper and computerized," Wayne LaPierre, executive vice president of the NRA, said on ABC Television's programme "This Week."

The federal government is already developing a nationwide screening system to collect state records of felons and fugitives to be used for screening gun purchasers. The programme is expected to be ready late next year.
"Majority Leader (Trent) Lott supports it, (House Speaker Newt) Gingrich supports it. The only one dragging their feet is the Justice Department and the White House, for some reason," LaPierre said.

Sarah Brady, an advocate for gun control since her husband James Brady was shot and wounded in an assassination attempt against President Ronald Reagan in 1981, said the NRA's argument was a "red herring" to try and dismantle the federally mandated waiting period.
A computerized system "is not going to be sufficient to run a really good, comprehensive background check," she said on the programme.
Brady also said that getting the system up and running would be difficult in some areas such as West Virginia, where she said some courthouses still store criminal records in shoe boxes.

Gun control supporters said last week's Supreme Court ruling would have little impact because most states already require background checks for gun purchasers. They claim that the Brady law, passed by Congress in 1993 as the toughest gun law in a generation, has stopped some 250,000 felons, fugitives or children from illegally buying guns.
